observations:
Torah 81 is a short, tightly unified teaching with one central metaphor: 'רגל' (foot) as the symbol of all lower spiritual levels that are capable of elevation through the joy of Torah and mitzvah. After thorough review of the source text and the complete bechina graph, no independent domain emerges that requires a new package beyond the two already identified.

The teaching has the following conceptual structure:

Package 1 (רגל — the lower levels, neutral): All the things that ARE called a 'regel' — netzach and hod (prophets), faith, wife, evil speech, money, son — form a coherent cluster of 'lower gradations.' This is the largest and most structurally central package.

Package 2 (צדק / Torah — the elevating force, good): Torah and mitzvah in their essential nature are צדק (righteousness), and צדק is the letter Heh (Shekhinah). The supporters of Torah are pillars of truth. This is the positive domain.

The Torah's argument is a single eitza arrow: Package 2 → (through joy) → Package 1 gets elevated. There is no third independent domain.

Potential candidates considered and rejected:

1. שמחה (joy) as a separate package: Joy is mentioned throughout as the mechanism, but the Rebbe never says 'X is a bechina of שמחה.' Joy functions purely as an eitza (cause) that elevates the feet. It is not defined by bechina equivalences with other concepts, and thus forms no package.

2. לב / חכמה as a separate package: The 'heart of wisdom' (לבב חכמה) is the destination, but the Rebbe does not develop it with multiple bechina equalities in this Torah. It is named once as the higher state, not elaborated into a cluster of 3+ nodes.

3. Evil mirror package: The Torah mentions 'דיבור הרע' (evil speech) as a 'regel,' but this does not constitute an evil counterpart package — the Rebbe does not develop an evil domain here. Evil speech is included within the neutral 'regel' cluster as one of many things that gets elevated, not as a counterforce with its own network of bechina relationships.

The dataset for this Torah is sparse relative to the text's richness, but the sparseness reflects genuine brevity of bechina statements in the source — most of the Torah's connections are eitza (cause-effect: joy causes elevation). The two packages identified fully exhaust the bechina topology of the teaching.
